I think that split seems to be okay and one could map the existing transactions into it the following way: Regular transaction: - code: empty - data: optionally set Creation transaction: - code: set - data: empty Rich tx: - code: set - data: optionally set Also <@!543900561460822016> regarding unobservability of gas there's this interesting idea from https://ethresear.ch/t/counter-proposal-to-oil-karma-per-account-gas-limits/7433: > Option 1: Allow a transaction to specify a table T: {account: gaslimit}. A call to an account A in T would only be assigned a maximum of T[A] gas, and otherwise calls would be assigned all the remaining gas. I think that could work well with this flag based transaction format. I'd call this the `AccountGasLimits` list, which is mutually exclusive with `GasLimit`. The `GasLimit` sets the limit for the account specified by the signature. I keep some notes here: https://hackmd.io/CccouoTaRUu8gCrFPLB1fg thanks for recording that info <@!425279588009246720> The number of use cases still feel quite slim 🙂 Personally, I am really hoping to be convinced of the long-term viability of Rich Transactions so I can drop interest/support in all of the alternatives. At least one thing we can agree on is that sponsoring is needed unless AA would be introduced. yes > I keep some notes here: https://hackmd.io/CccouoTaRUu8gCrFPLB1fg Thanks <@!425279588009246720> Sponsoring and an account "doing multiple things in a row" are the two features that I think we all agree need to be solved for. <@!543900561460822016> are you adamant on having multi-sender in the batching (outside of richtx) ? <@!425279588009246720> Where is that hackmd where you were putting together all of the various options? Not the one linked above, the other one. If we can make sponsoring txs and doing multiple things in in a row in berlin, I would be more than happy to champion that effort (w/o multi-sender batching) https://notes.ethereum.org/@axic/Hyrc1i7ED and generally, its not a hill i want to die on, but if we're looking beyond berlin, i'd like to implement both <@!301186049323958275> actually started writing an alternative to 2711, but figured out the notation isn't all that bad, just hard to understand first 🙂 Oh, the other use case <@!543900561460822016> was create2 from EOA. > Oh, the other use case <@!543900561460822016> was create2 from EOA. Right, that's a new one. Is create2 from EOA that useful? I would think we'd want to use a deployer contract anyways? There's no need for a deployer if you can do it from an EOA. yes, but what is the use case for doing so from an EOA (besides the small gas savings) The same as doing it through a deployer/proxy: to use create2 functionality. It simplifies things a bit, though not much in the common case. It does give every user their own "namespace", but that is pretty marginal. yeah, agreed that the benefit is very marginal ~~Conditional executions are another use case.~~ Though, really that is just more of the "breaking `isHuman` checks" I guess. > https://notes.ethereum.org/@axic/Hyrc1i7ED Based on this I have two changes to 2711: - Split code and data fields (this has the further benefit of not analyzing EVM bytecode twice, e.g. as part of the deployer vs. as part of deployed code) - Introduce a flag based encoding This is what I'm writing as an EIP, just did not found too much time this week. As someone with a contract wallet, I'm extremely annoyed that I cannot use my wallet with a bunch of contracts out there because of `isHuman` checks and similar, which is why I push so hard to break them. Why do people do `isHuman` checks? Primarily because they are trying to protect against conditional execution. That is, they don't want people taking some action only if certain conditions are met. e.g., "do X if timestamp is after Y". When really it just says, "this contract is insecure, but only miners can exploit this contract". The other is rollups, because they want to ensure that transaction `data` field is laid out a particular way so they don't have to inspect the transaction. > The other is rollups, because they want to ensure that transaction `data` field is laid out a particular way so they don't have to inspect the transaction. How is this related? A contract cannot trust the data no matter whether it is part of the an EOA or `CALL` calldata. <@!543900561460822016> I suspect the root of our disagreement comes mostly down to complexity. If you ignore multi-sender sponsored transactions and I ignore `isHuman` breakage, then I think you still prefer batch because you think it is lower complexity and I prefer rich because I think it is lower complexity. With rollups, Etehreum is the data availability layer. They achieve this cheaply by including all of the rollup data in the transaction's calldata, which the layer 2 chain then parses and operates on. I think complexity is comparable just differs at where the complexity lies at. And richtx has the potential to be more flexible. On layer 1, that data is just hashed and aggregated essentially. On layer 2, that data is calldata for a contract execution. The layer 2 chain has it slightly easier if they can just look at the layer 1 transaction list for any transactions with a `to` field for their rollup contract and then just read the `data`. If contracts were allowed to call into the rollup contract on layer 1, then they would have to simulate every transaction to find the rollup calls (since they could be internal). Contracts **are** allowed to call rollup contracts. Not needing an EVM (just something that speaks devp2p) does have its appeal. Sure, they can "reject" incoming transactions, but they can't reject incoming coinbase/selfdestruct. > Contracts **are** allowed to call rollup contracts. Not all of them. Not sure why rollup people would want to solve user error really. It isn't solving user error in this case. It is making their tooling development easier. If their rules state "we only parse EOA calldata and ignore anything else" then it doesn't matter if someone tries to call it. It is user error, ignored by L2. Maybe this is too pragmatic for users 😬 The rollup contract needs to *not* rollup the transaction. Otherwise the transaction list rollup won't match the layer 2 transaction list. 🤔 Though, perhaps you are saying that the transaction would still show up in the L2 transaction list, it would just be executed as a no-op? I don't think that would work because you would still need to *see* that transaction to know to turn it into a no-op. I guess you could fire a really lightweight event so you at least know *something* was rolled up, but you can turn it into a no-op if it wasn't a direct call from an EOA. Wait a second, isn't the batching/checkpointing on L1 done by trusted nodes from L2 anyway? Not in a good rollup. 🙂 Some of the crappier ones do that. 😛 (highly opinionated hot take) The most censorship resistant/trustless way to do a rollup is to have every transaction sent directly to layer 1, and those are executed (in order they appeared on layer 1) on layer 2. Though I'd argue they should look at emitted events and consider that as canon, and not transactions lists. Emitting an event increases gas costs pretty significantly, almost 2x I think? Most of the cost on L1 is the calldata payload size IIRC. Stuffing all that into an event increases that portion. Sure, they either improve their tooling (support executing transactions) or pay more gas, right? FWIW, I am not a fan of the `isHuman` checks for rollups. It is just "the other case for `ishuman`". The system is so convoluted due to all the workarounds added in order to keep "everyone happy", when it should be recognized that it is not possible to keep everyone happy and we just dig deeper in complexity with trying to avoid that. <@!543900561460822016> why do you think the `AccountGasLimit` list is a bad solution compared to tx-level batching? it just feels like a workaround, further increasing the evm complexity I think `AccountGasLimits` could be nice in general. Would have to come with making `GAS` return ~0 and `CALL` ignoring gas limits. fair enough, i don't have a strong argument against it other than it just *feels* unnecessarily obtuse It does feel like more "brutal" and not fine-tuned, not sure if that is a problem. What is AccountGasLimit? option 1 from this post: https://ethresear.ch/t/counter-proposal-to-oil-karma-per-account-gas-limits/7433 Actually the messy part of it is that one would need to maintain that list an continuously deduct form it. I wonder if the main thing needed would be `GasLimit` and `CallGasLimit` or `ReservedGasLimit`, where the goal is to keep some extra gas for `depth = 0`, but ignore any further call depths. That is pretty constraining, means your logic *must* be at the root of the stack.

excerpts.author: axic3354
excerpts.content:
In the "rich tx ftw" section I propose to introduce a data/code field, whereas today there's only data which is used differently based on what the transaction is doing, i.e. if it is a creation transaction it is considered as code, otherwise as calldata.

I think that split seems to be okay and one could map the existing transactions into it the following way:

Regular transaction:
- code: empty
- data: optionally set

Creation transaction:
- code: set
- data: empty

Rich tx:
- code: set
- data: optionally set

excerpts.author: axic3354
excerpts.content:
Also <@!543900561460822016> regarding unobservability of gas there's this interesting idea from https://ethresear.ch/t/counter-proposal-to-oil-karma-per-account-gas-limits/7433: 

> Option 1: Allow a transaction to specify a table T: {account: gaslimit}. A call to an account A in T would only be assigned a maximum of T[A] gas, and otherwise calls would be assigned all the remaining gas.

I think that could work well with this flag based transaction format.

I'd call this the `AccountGasLimits` list, which is mutually exclusive with `GasLimit`. The `GasLimit` sets the limit for the account specified by the signature.
